title: IELTS Listening — Full-Length Original Practice (Audio Required)
description: Original 4-section, 40-question script-based practice draft. No recording is included. Do not publish until real recordings are attached and verified for all four sections.

listening.instructions: Four sections, 10 questions each. Allow 30 minutes for the recording and 10 minutes for answer transfer. Normal student use requires one verified recording per section.

parts.title: Section 1 — Riverside repair booking
parts.instructions: Two speakers: a customer arranges a bicycle repair with a service desk.
parts.recordingScript: CUSTOMER: I need to book my bicycle in. It is a green touring bike, not the blue road bike I brought last year. CLERK: What is the frame number? CUSTOMER: 48271. The front brake cable has frayed, and the rear tyre loses air overnight. CLERK: We can inspect both. The workshop is at 18 Willow Lane. The earliest appointment is Thursday the 14th at 9:30. CUSTOMER: I have a class then. Is Friday possible? CLERK: Friday the 15th, at 11:00. CUSTOMER: That works. Please use my mobile ending 6042. CLERK: The inspection costs £12, payable when you collect it. If we need parts, we will call before doing extra work. CUSTOMER: I will bring the lock key too. CLERK: Please leave the bicycle by the side entrance, not the front counter.

parts.title: Section 2 — Bellmere wetland visitor route
parts.instructions: A guide gives visitors information about a nature reserve.
parts.recordingScript: GUIDE: Welcome to Bellmere Wetland. The visitor centre opens at 8:30, and the last entry is 4:15. Please begin at the east gate because the north gate is closed for repairs this month. The blue route is 2.4 kilometres and takes about 50 minutes. The shorter reed-bed loop is 1.1 kilometres, but it is closed after heavy rain. Binoculars can be borrowed at the information desk for a refundable deposit of five pounds. The observation tower is the best place to see herons, especially before midday. The café is beside the old pump house, not inside the visitor centre. At 10:00 and 2:00, a ranger leads a free walk from the map board. Dogs are welcome only on the gravel path and must remain on a lead. Please do not feed the ducks; bread can harm them. The accessible toilet is behind the education room.

parts.title: Section 3 — Student research project meeting
parts.instructions: Two students and a tutor discuss a university research project.
parts.recordingScript: TUTOR: Your project is about how students use quiet study rooms. What have you done so far? MAYA: We planned to interview staff, but the booking system already provides useful room-occupancy data. LEO: We will still interview students about why they choose particular rooms. TUTOR: How many responses do you have? MAYA: The pilot survey had 18 responses. We revised two confusing questions and sent the final survey to three departments; it closes on the 22nd. LEO: We will compare morning and evening use, but we should not claim that room design causes a preference. TUTOR: Correct. Your sample is self-selected. What about the presentation? MAYA: I will make the charts. LEO: I will write the limitations section and check the references. MAYA: We both need to explain the method. TUTOR: Use the seminar room projector, but bring a backup PDF on a USB drive. The library printer is unreliable. LEO: We should meet on Tuesday at 3:15 to rehearse. TUTOR: Good. Your report is due on the 30th, not the 28th listed on the old course page.

parts.title: Section 4 — Repair cafés and product life
parts.instructions: A lecturer explains a small study of community repair cafés.
parts.recordingScript: LECTURER: A repair café is a community event where volunteers help residents fix household objects. Our study followed four cafés in the fictional region of Eastmere for six months. Volunteers recorded the item, the fault, and whether it was repaired, but did not record visitors’ names. The most common items were lamps, small kitchen appliances, and clothing. Electrical items were tested with a portable safety meter after repair. About 62 percent of all items were repaired during the visit; another 14 percent needed a part that the café did not have. The organisers found that a clear booking form reduced waiting time more effectively than adding extra tables. However, the study cannot show how long repaired objects remained in use. A follow-up survey is planned for next spring. The team recommends publishing repair instructions with photographs, because several volunteers reported that written steps alone were difficult to follow. It also recommends separating safety checks from cosmetic improvements. The regional grant will fund tools, but not permanent staff. Further research should compare rural and urban events, since transport to a café may be a barrier for some residents.
